analysis.one_liner: Bans price gouging of gasoline and diesel in federally declared disaster areas, enforced by the FTC.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee on September 14, 2005, it saw no further action before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a major disaster is declared, the bill would make it unlawful to sell gasoline or diesel in that area for more than 10% above the average price of the previous 30 days — unless the seller could show the increase came from real added costs, like higher replacement, tax, or transport expenses, or matched national or international market trends. The ban would last 90 days after the disaster declaration, and the Federal Trade Commission would enforce it as an unfair or deceptive practice. The FTC would also have to post the pre-disaster average prices on its website within five days, so consumers and enforcers would know the baseline. State price-gouging laws would stay in place. The bill came right after Hurricane Katrina, when fuel prices spiked across the Gulf Coast.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and households in areas hit by federally or state-declared disasters — the people filling tanks during emergencies like hurricanes — would gain a federal backstop against pump prices jumping more than 10% over the pre-disaster average, with the FTC policing violations and posting the baseline prices online so the numbers are checkable.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for a vendor to sell gasoline or diesel at 10% or more above the area's average price from the 30 days before a disaster declaration, unless the increase reflects real added costs or matches national or international market trends.
Gives the FTC enforcement power, treating a violation as an unfair or deceptive practice under the FTC Act, so consumers have a federal enforcement route rather than depending only on state laws.
Requires the FTC to post the area's pre-disaster average gasoline and diesel prices on its website within five days of a declaration, so consumers and enforcers know the baseline being used.
Preserves state price-gouging laws, letting states keep their own protections except where directly inconsistent.

analysis.who_pays: Gasoline retailers, refiners, and wholesalers selling in declared disaster areas, who would have to hold prices within 10% of the pre-disaster average or document real added costs, and face FTC enforcement if they did not.

drawbacks.text: The 10% trigger is blunt: a filling station facing genuinely higher replacement, tax, or transportation costs after a storm could exceed the threshold and have to prove its costs were reasonable, which could discourage some vendors from shipping extra fuel into a damaged area when it is needed most.

The prohibition is temporary and narrow — 90 days, only in federally or state-declared disaster areas, with exceptions for costs and market-wide trends — so it does nothing about sustained high gasoline prices outside disasters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a federal floor against price spikes in disaster zones, with a published baseline price so consumers and enforcers can check the math — is real but narrow: it applies for 90 days after a disaster declaration, only in declared areas, and it has escape valves for genuine cost increases and normal market swings, so the 10% rule would rarely punish ordinary market movement. The costs an honest supporter would acknowledge are real: a rigid price ceiling during a supply shock can discourage vendors from trucking extra fuel into a damaged area (the "reasonable additional cost" exemption tries to cover this but invites arguments), and the FTC would be handed a new enforcement workload on short deadlines. On balance it is a modest, targeted consumer protection whose main drawback is that it was never tested — it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee, where it stayed until the 109th Congress ended, never getting a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 14, 2005, referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection on September 19, 2005.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded for the bill before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
It carried bipartisan support from the start, with 28 cosponsors (15 Republicans and 13 Democrats) joining Republican sponsor Heather Wilson of New Mexico.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fuel sellers, refiners, and wholesalers keep the ability to raise prices sharply in declared disaster areas without a federal price-gouging limit or FTC enforcement, and the committee that held the bill faced no recorded vote on it.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill across both parties.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in its action history.

against.name: Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 19, 2005 and recorded no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor joined by 15 Republican and 13 Democratic cosponsors — so its death in committee was not a party-line vote; no vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: Petroleum refiners and wholesale fuel suppliers
industries.note: The bill's price limit applies to commercial vendors selling gasoline and diesel in disaster areas, and its exceptions cover costs 'imposed by the vendor's source,' so a spike traced to refiner or wholesale prices could be challenged downstream. Refiners could no longer pass through windfall pricing to disaster-zone consumers for 90 days after a declaration.

Retailers in a declared disaster area could not raise pump prices more than 10% above the pre-disaster 30-day average unless they could show real added costs or a market-wide trend, enforced by the FTC. This removes the ability to reprice freely during the exact periods when drivers have the fewest alternatives.
